chapter: Bands and bandleading in New Orleans
title: Machine shop business and the Coast Guard in the war
summary: The war draft pulled his business staff; he served in the Coast Guard, where he sat in with service bands but could not get in one.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: That's about the time I left Joe's Inn and the war came on. Yeah. We had the little business and before you know it all of the personnel that actually ran the business was in A1 classification with the draft board. I was the last one so I got a little deformity until I got somebody broken in to run the business. There's another case like music. I had a machine shop. I had a business. Just like music. But they were setting other guys up building machine shops for them and putting them in business so they could stay and make money. And I went. So I didn't take a bite. I'm still patriotic despite the way things are going. I guess I'd go again if I could. And during the war I couldn't get in any Coast Guard. I was in the Coast Guard. They had a nice band over, a big old band though. Something like the Blue Room Band over at St. Augustine. I saw old Roy Zinnerman over there, St. Augustine. He was playing with that band, with the Coast Guard Band. I was transferred to Galveston and they had an unrated band there but they got out of all the hard work and it was hard to get in too because I'd go around there and sit in and think that maybe I might get in the band and they'd be doing Guard Duty, you know?
